analog: Penicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in hospitals after penicillin's introduction (Hammersmith Hospital, London, 1946-1948), to methicillin (1959) and MRSA (1961)

threat.doubling_time_notes: Derived here, not published: fitting a logistic through 12.5% (Apr 1946) and 38% (Jun 1947) gives growth rate r = 1.245/yr, so ln2/r = 0.56 years (the early-phase doubling used by L.logistic). The fit predicts ~56% at Jan 1948 vs 59% reported, a good check. Use L.logistic(t, 0.56, s0) with s0 chosen so the curve passes 0.125 at t=0 (equivalent to starting the clock earlier).
threat.notes: extent = share of S. aureus isolates from hospital patients at Hammersmith that were penicillin-resistant. One hospital, not the world; label accordingly. The month of the 59% figure is assumed from the 1948 publication; value itself is sourced.

aggregation.notes: Derived from documented dates (years after Apr 1946), not a measured distribution: p10 = Barber's warning (~1947-48, s1), median = new drug in clinical use (methicillin 1959, s5), p90 = global coordinated plan (2015, s6, unverified). Resistance to the new drug followed within ~2 years (1961).

deploy.notes: Methicillin 1959 to first MRSA reports 1961: how long the deployed fix held before red caught up.

ai_counterfactual.basis: Illustrative, and only for the coordination fragment. Barber's hospital data were ready by ~1947-48; turning surveillance from many hospitals into a routed prescribing/infection-control policy is analysis and communication work well inside the ~17.4 h 50% task horizon in RATES.md (METR entry), repeated cheaply across hospitals per RATES.md 'Cost of AI at fixed capability'. Assumed: a stewardship response assembled ~1 year after the warning (t=2.5) instead of the ~13-year median. This does NOT assume faster drug development: RATES.md's 'Science example' shows design can be days, but trials and manufacturing still take years, and bacteria keep evolving.
ai_counterfactual.label: illustrative

gap_summary: Resistant hospital staph went from 1 in 8 to nearly 6 in 10 in under two years (odds doubling ~every 7 months); the new drug took ~13 years and was itself beaten in 2.
